newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus govt spends $20 mln of IMF loan on fuel.
newsitem.headline: Belarus govt spends $20 mln of IMF loan on fuel.

text.p: Belarus has taken $20 million from an International Monetary Fund loan intended to support gold and hard currency reserves to spend on oil, the head of the state energy concern said on Thursday.
Anton Loiko, who heads Belnefteprodukt, told Reuters the government had passed on the cash as higher prices in the West had drawn Russian fuel oil producers away.
"In January-September our two major plants refined 35,000 to 40,000 tonnes of oil in 24 hours but in the last few weeks that has fallen to just 22,000 tonnes," he said.
Loiko said an increase in world oil prices to around $160 a tonne was drawing Russian exports away from Belarus -- where prices are much lower because of a customs union agreement.
"Russian producers are sending all their oil to the West, in transit across Belarus, where they would only raise $93 to $95 a tonne," he said.
As a result, Loiko said, the cabinet of ministers had ordered the cash to be taken for fuel oil reserves from the first, $70 million tranche of a $250 million stand-by loan.
Another $30 million of the tranche was spent in April -- to buy fertiliser for collective farms.
The IMF has frozen the rest of the credit pending speedier reforms in the republic sandwiched between Russian and Poland.
An IMF official in Minsk said the Fund was unaware of the government decision.
When the Fund paid the tranche in September 1995, it recommended it be used to support gold and currency reserves.

"The Fund has always stressed that a regulated currency, regulated prices and a lack of privatisation mean talks cannot be held with Belarus on continuing IMF credits," the official, who asked not to be named, said.

President Alexander Lukashenko, who has frozen the country's privatisation programme, on Thursday appointed Vasily Novak minister of privatisation and state property, filling a post which had been vacant for over a year.
The IMF official also said Lukashenko's currency policies were making life tough for Russian oil producers.
A presidential decree keeps the Belarussian currency within 13,000-15,500 to the dollar on the interbank market, and only about half the demand for the U.S. currency is being met.
"Russian oil companies cannot convert the profits to hard currency because of severe limitations on the hard currency market," he said.
